latin: Ludovice! Nōbīscum veniās oportet<sup>1</sup>!
Quid accidit? Quid negōtiī<sup>2</sup> vōs tantopere urget<sup>3</sup>?
Hodiē vespere apud avunculum Gregorium saltātiōnem<sup>4</sup> īnstituēmus<sup>5</sup>.
Cōnsōbrīnae nostrae Claudia et Caecilia adērunt. Multum oblectābimur<sup>6</sup>.
Saltātiōnī nōn studeō<sup>7</sup>. Claudiam et Caeciliam ōdī<sup>8</sup>. Germānae<sup>9</sup> sunt pestēs: omnēs et omnia semper rōdunt<sup>10</sup>.
Saltāre nōn cōgeris, nec cum eīs colloquī.
Exquīsītae mēnsae appōnentur in eīsque cibī et pōtiōnēs maximā varietāte: acipensērīs<sup>11</sup> ōva, pernae, crustulārumque omne genus<sup>12</sup>.
Frūstrā mē tentābis. Nec bibāx nec edāx<sup>13</sup> sum.
Mūsicane dēlectāris?
Mūsica dēlector, sed ōtium mihi deest eī operam dandī.
Nīsī<sup>14</sup> vēnerīs, concentus absurdus erit. Mārcellus tubā canit, ego tympanum pulsāre possum,
Sed nēminem<sup>15</sup> praeter tē inveniō quī clavichordīō canere possit.
Cūr hoc prīmum nōn dīxistī? Clavichordīō vestrī grātiā canam.
Pergrātum mihi est amīcīs ūtilem esse.
latinAccented: Ludóvice! Nōbī́scum véniās opórtet<sup>1</sup>!
Quid áccidit? Quid negṓtiī<sup>2</sup> vōs tantópere urget<sup>3</sup>?
Hódiē véspere apud avúnculum Gregórium saltātiṓnem<sup>4</sup> īnstituḗmus<sup>5</sup>.
Cōnsōbrī́nae nostrae Cláudia et Caecília adḗrunt. Multum oblectā́bimur<sup>6</sup>.
Saltātiṓnī nōn stúdeō<sup>7</sup>. Cláudiam et Caecíliam ōdī<sup>8</sup>. Germā́nae<sup>9</sup> sunt pestēs: omnēs et ómnia semper rōdunt<sup>10</sup>.
Saltā́re nōn cṓgeris, nec cum eīs cólloquī.
Exquīsī́tae mēnsae appōnéntur in eī́sque cibī et pōtiṓnēs máximā varietā́te: acipensḗrīs<sup>11</sup> ōva, pernae, crustulārúmque omne genus<sup>12</sup>.
Frūstrā mē tentā́bis. Nec bibāx nec edāx<sup>13</sup> sum.
Mūsicáne dēlectā́ris?
Mū́sica dēléctor, sed ṓtium mihi deest eī óperam dandī.
Nīsī<sup>14</sup> vḗnerīs, concéntus absúrdus erit. Mārcéllus tubā canit, ego týmpanum pulsā́re possum,
Sed nḗminem<sup>15</sup> praeter tē invéniō quī clavichordī́ō cánere possit.
Cūr hoc prīmum nōn dīxístī? Clavichordī́ō vestrī grā́tiā canam.
Pergrā́tum mihi est amī́cīs ū́tilem esse.
english: Louis! You must come with us (it-is-required you-should-come with-us)!
What happens (of an incident)? What [business] (of-business) is pressing you so much?
[This] (today) evening at uncle Gregory's we will be holding a surprise party (dance we-will-set-up).
Our cousins Claudia and Cecilia will be there. [We will have great fun] (much we-will-be-amused).
I have no interest in dancing. I hate Claudia and Cecilia. They are real pests: they always [backbite about] (nibble) everyone and everything.
You won't be forced to dance, nor to speak with them.

[There will be a great buffet with the most varied foods and drinks] (Exquisite tables will be served up and on them foods and drinks in the greatest variety): [caviar] (sturgeon's eggs), hams, and every kind of cakes (cf. L 19, P 4).
You (will) tempt me in vain. I'm neither very given to drink nor gluttonous.
[Do you enjoy music] (by-music are-you-pleased)?
I enjoy music, but [I have no time to pay attention to it] (leisure to-me is-lacking to-it attention of-giving).
Unless [you come] (you-will-have-come), the symphony will be out of tune. Marcel [plays] the trumpet (with-trumpet sings); myself, I can beat the drum;
but [except for you I can find] nobody (except you I-find) who can play the piano.
Why didn't you say this first? I'll play the piano [for your sake] (by-grace of-you[pl.]).
It is most agreeable for me to be useful to [my] friends.

footnotes: Oportet, an impersonal verb that we've already seen in the infinitive (oportere) in Lesson 13 (P. 9). It is construed with the conjunction ut and the subjunctive: oportet ut venias, it is required that you come. Ut can be omitted, as here in phrase 1, but the subjunctive is compulsory.
Quid negotii, word for word what of the business. We could have said quod negotium, but this latter expression would have been less appropriate.

Urgeo, -es, -ere, -ursi (2nd conjugation, no supine), to push forward, press (literally or figuratively); cf. English urgent. Tantopere, so much, adv., derived from an ablative tanto opere, literally by so much work.
Saltatio, -onis, f., dance, from saltare, to dance. To jump (French sauter, cf. English somersault) is salire, a 4th-conjugation verb that we'll see again.
Instituo, -is, -ere, -ui, -utum, to set up, to organize (future ind. instituam, institues, instituet, instituemus, instituetis, instituent).

Oblectare (active voice), to amuse. Oblectari (passive voice), to be amused, to amuse oneself. The verbs of the 1st conjugation (active inf. in -are and passive in -ari) make the future in -bo, -bis, -bit, -bimus, -bitis, -bunt in the active; and in -bor, -beris, -bitur, -bimur, -bimini, -buntur in the passive; we'll come back to this.
Studeo, -es, -ere, -ui + dat., to have a taste for; to study is a secondary meaning: studet algebrae, he studies algebra.
Odi, I hate, I detest, just like memini, I remember, has a perfect form but a present meaning (I've taken a dislike to); you hate is thus odisti, he hates odit, they hate oderunt.
Germanus, -a, -um, comes from germen, -inis, n., sprout. Frater germanus, full brother, whence figuratively true, real.
Rodo, -is, -ere, rosi, rosum, to gnaw. Its derivatives erodere and corrodere have given us erode and erosion on the one hand, and corrode and corrosion on the other.
Acipenser, -eris, m., sturgeon, from whose eggs caviar is made (you can forget this word if you wish).
Genus, -eris, n., origin, race, sort: a word to retain!
Bibax, -acis, adj. is derived from bibere, just as edax comes from edere, to eat. Adjectives in -ax indicate a propensity, generally excessive.

Nemo (acc. neminem, dat. nemini, not used in other cases), nobody (m. and f.). [Long note excised on the difference between nemo and French personne, which requires an added negative particle ne]. In Latin, as in algebra and standard English, two negatives to cancel, yielding a positive sense. This is true in a first approach, for, if we go bit deeper, the double negative is not always the exact equivalent of an affirmation…
comments: Attention! Using the translation, check that you understand well phrases 6 and 11 of the exercise. If you immediately put the various nouns in their proper place (direct object, possessive phrase) it means you already have the Latin spirit. If you are not there yet, do not forget often to repeat this sort of exercise: what seems to you still to be artificial will become completely natural little by little. Think of: consuetudinis magna vis (L 29, P 11).

latin: Quis mēcum saltātum venit?
Nēmō tēcum saltāre vult.
Quae tam bene saltat?
Quis mūsica dēlectātur? — Nēmō mūsica nōn dēlectātur.
Cave canem! — Ubi est canis?
Canis dominum nōn videō.
Ā cane nunc mordētur. Ā cane heri morsus est.
Canis eum momordit.
Canī pernam dare nōlī.
Canēs quī plūrimum lātrant, rārō mordent.
Sīmius cānum cibum fūrātus est.
Ā multīs canibus morsae sunt.

Quis mū́sica dēlectā́tur? — Nēmō mū́sica nōn dēlectā́tur.

Canis dóminum nōn vídeō.
Ā cane nunc mordḗtur. Ā cane heri morsus est.

Canī pernam dare nōlī.

english: Who is coming to dance with me?
No one wants to dance with you.
Which one (female) dances so well?
Who enjoys music? — No one does not enjoy music.
Beware [of] the dog! — Where is the dog?
I don't see the dog's master.
Now he is bitten by a dog. Yesterday he was bitten by a dog.
A dog bit him.
[Don't give] ham to the dog (to-give do-not-want).
Dogs who bark the most, rarely bite.
The monkey stole the dogs' food.
They (f.) were bitten by many dogs.
